Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Apex EV Inc. Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers’ presentation, there will be a question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question at that time, please press star then one on your touchtone phone. If you're using a speakerphone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. To withdraw your question, press star then two. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Johnson, VP of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Johnson:
Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex EV Inc.'s Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me today are Alex Rivera, CEO; Mike Chen, CFO; and other members of our leadership team.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by these statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. Q3 was a pivotal quarter for Apex EV Inc. We made significant strides in key areas, including ramping production volumes and capacity utilization rates to new highs amid supply chain resilience, implementing targeted pricing strategies and promotional activities to drive market share gains, driving down battery costs per kWh through vertical integration and chemistry optimizations, and expanding our charging network with improved utilization rates to support customer adoption. We are particularly excited about the upcoming launch of the Apex X crossover and its anticipated 15% boost to our market share in the premium SUV segment.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Mike Chen to discuss our financial performance in more detail.

Mike Chen:
Thank you, Alex. Good morning, everyone. For Q3, our revenue was $7.3 billion, representing a 22% increase year-over-year. Our gross margin was 20.5%, reflecting a balance of volume growth and cost efficiencies, and our operating expenses were $1.4 billion. Net income was $520 million. We are maintaining a strong balance sheet with $5.2 billion in cash and cash equivalents and $18 billion in total liquidity. Our guidance for next quarter is revenue of $8.0 to $8.5 billion, with gross margins expanding to 21-22%.

I'll now turn to our production volumes and capacity utilization rates, which continue to reflect the strong execution of our vertical integration strategy amid a dynamic EV landscape. In Q3, we achieved total vehicle production of 305,000 units, marking a 32% year-over-year increase and a 12% sequential improvement from Q2. This performance underscores our ability to scale efficiently, even as the broader industry grapples with softening demand in Europe and battery raw material volatility.

Breaking it down by segment, our core SUV lineup—led by the Apex Apex and Apex Pro platforms, our direct competitors to Tesla's Model Y and Rivian's R1S—accounted for 62% of output at 189,000 units, up 38% YoY. This ramp was fueled by robust North American demand, where incentives under the IRA have boosted fleet orders from partners like Hertz and Enterprise. Our pickup segment, anchored by the all-new Thunderbolt, delivered 85,000 units, a 48% YoY surge as we capture share from Ford's F-150 Lightning and GM's Silverado EV in the light-duty truck market. Sedan production, primarily the Quantum series targeting the BYD Seal and Hyundai Ioniq 6 space, came in at 31,000 units, up slightly YoY following inventory management ahead of our next-gen refresh with 800V architecture.

On capacity utilization, we averaged 90% across our global footprint, up from 76% in Q3 last year and 87% in Q2. This is a testament to our disciplined CapEx allocation—$1.5 billion deployed YTD on targeted expansions—and operational efficiencies like our proprietary AI-driven dynamic line balancing, which has reduced changeover times by 22%. Nameplate capacity now stands at 1.1 million units annually, with headroom for 1.3 million by year-end following the Phase 2 ramp at our Texas Gigafactory.

Regionally, North America led with 94% utilization at our Fremont-adjacent Nevada and Texas facilities, producing 180,000 units. The Texas site hit 97% on Thunderbolt lines, benefiting from localized 4680 cell production that cut battery costs by 20% QoQ and mitigated supply risks from CATL delays. Europe, at 82% utilization from our Berlin Gigafactory, produced 70,000 units but faced headwinds from subsidy phase-outs in Germany and France, echoing Volkswagen's ID.4 struggles—our response includes a 20% ASP premium pivot to premium trims. In China, Shanghai utilization reached 93% for 55,000 units, leveraging LFP cell localization to counter BYD's price wars; exports to APAC grew 50% YoY, targeting Thailand's EV3.5 incentives.

Key technical initiatives driving these metrics include our vertical integration of structural battery packs, now at 45 GWh annual capacity, reducing WH/mi by 12% to 240 on Apex models and enabling 500-mile range. We've also deployed 150 ABB robots per line for gigacasting, mirroring Tesla's unboxed process, which boosted throughput 25% while cutting defects to under 50 PPM. Supply chain resilience remains core: dual-sourcing nickel from Indonesia and lithium from our Nevada JV has de-risked 85% of our pack BOM.

Strategically, we're prioritizing mix shift toward high-margin trucks and SUVs, now 80% of production, to deliver 25% gross margins in Q4. Challenges persist—semiconductor shortages trimmed 5,000 units, and softening EU demand caps utilization there at 75-80% through Q4—but our $2.5 billion FY CapEx plan, 60% on U.S. capacity, positions us for 1.2 million full-year production guidance, a 35% YoY increase.

Looking ahead, Q4 volumes are guided at 330,000-340,000 units with 92-94% utilization, scaling to 95%+ as Thunderbolt hits full rate. This trajectory supports our ambition to close the gap with Tesla's 1.8 million run-rate while outpacing legacy OEMs in EV purity.

Before we open the floor to questions, I'd like to dive deeper into one of the key drivers behind our results: the impact of our pricing strategies and promotional activities. As you know, the EV market remains fiercely competitive, with intensifying price pressures from legacy OEMs like Ford and GM accelerating their EV ramps, Chinese hyperscalers such as BYD and NIO flooding export markets, and macroeconomic headwinds like elevated interest rates softening consumer demand. Our approach has been deliberate—balancing volume growth and market share gains with margin discipline—and it's delivering results amid these dynamics.

In Q3, we executed targeted price adjustments across our portfolio, including a 12% ASP reduction on our flagship Apex S sedan—now starting at $48,900 after incentives—and introductory pricing on the new Apex X crossover at $62,500, undercutting Rivian's R2 by about 8% on a feature-adjusted basis. These moves, combined with aggressive promotional campaigns, drove a 28% quarter-over-quarter increase in retail deliveries to 142,000 units globally, helping us capture 4.2% U.S. EV market share, up from 3.1% in Q2. However, this came at the cost of a 310 basis point contraction in vehicle gross margins to 18.4%, primarily from mix shift toward higher-volume, lower-ASP models and promo-related revenue deferrals.

To quantify this, our global Average Selling Price (ASP) fell 9.2% sequentially to $51,200, reflecting a 15% YoY decline in China due to localized pricing parity with BYD's Seagull at RMB 69,800 (~$9,800 USD equivalent); stable U.S. ASPs at $55,400, bolstered by IRA-compliant configurations qualifying for the full $7,500 tax credit; and a 7% drop in Europe to €48,200 (~$52,000 USD), as we absorbed subsidy phase-outs in Germany and France.

Promotional activities amplified these effects. Our 'Zero-to-60 in Zero Payments' campaign—offering 0% APR financing for 72 months on Apex S leases—saw a 45% take rate, up from 22% in Q2, contributing to a 35% surge in U.S. leasing penetration to 42% of retail sales. Trade-in bonuses averaging $4,200 per vehicle cleared 18,000 units of prior-gen inventory, improving channel stock from 68 to 42 days' supply. Referral programs, enhanced with 12 months of free SuperCharge access (valued at $1,200), generated 12,500 incremental orders at a customer acquisition cost of just $450—30% below industry benchmarks from Cox Automotive data.

On the P&L, these initiatives boosted top-line revenue by 22% YoY to $7.3 billion, with promotions accounting for ~$850 million in direct incentives. Net impact on gross profit was a $420 million headwind, or 5.8% of revenue, but this was partially offset by cost-out initiatives like battery cell costs down 22% YoY to $85/kWh via our expanded Nevada Gigafactory output and LFP cathode sourcing from CATL; regulatory tailwinds including $320 million in U.S. IRA credits and European ZEV mandate sales; and upsell levers where FSD take rate climbed to 28% (from 24% in Q2) thanks to bundled pricing at $8,000, adding $1.1 billion in high-margin software revenue.

Regionally, our strategies were tailored to local dynamics: In North America (62% of deliveries), U.S. pricing held firm amid Tesla's iterative cuts, but our promo stack—including $2,999 lease cash and fleet deals with Hertz—flipped fleet sales to 15% of volume, up from 8%. This de-risked demand softness from high rates, with lease residuals holding at 58% after 36 months per Black Book valuations. In China (22% of deliveries), hyper-competitive pricing war intensified, with our Qin Plus rival priced at RMB 129,900 to match BYD's volume leader. Promos like 5-year free OTA updates drove 41% YoY growth, but ASP compression squeezed margins to 12.1%. We're countering with vertical integration, targeting 15% cost reduction in Q4 via Shanghai plant efficiencies. In Europe (12% of deliveries), subsidy cliffs post-€9,000 German cuts forced a 10% price reset, paired with CO2 credit sales yielding €150 million. Leasing promos at 1.9% APR captured urban fleet buyers, lifting market share to 3.8% vs. VW ID.3. In APAC/Other (4%), selective entry pricing in Australia and Japan, with 0% downpayment promos, yielded 55% YoY growth despite right-hand-drive tooling costs.

Looking ahead, our pricing philosophy is 'value-based penetration'—not commoditization. We've layered in technical differentiators to protect premiums: dynamic pricing via Apex AI, with real-time elasticity modeling adjusts MSRPs by up to 5% regionally, based on 2.5 million data points from our app ecosystem—early tests show 12% uplift in conversion rates; software-margin flywheel where Q3 bundling of Apex Autonomy Suite (Level 3-capable) with hardware discounts increased ARPU by $2,800 per vehicle, with roadmap including Q4 V12.5 update rivaling Tesla FSD v12; and inventory optimization where promo cadence now algorithmically tied to 45-day supply targets, reducing aged stock write-downs by 60% YoY.

For Q4, we expect ASP stabilization at $52,500 (±3%), with volume guidance of 155,000-165,000 units for retail deliveries. Promos will moderate to 4.5% of ASP, targeting 19.5-20.5% gross margins as new Apex X ramps (with 500+ mile LFP packs) shift mix upward. Risks include further China deflation—BYD's recent 10% cuts signal potential 20% industry ASP erosion—but our $18 billion liquidity and 48% vertical integration provide buffers. This disciplined approach positions us for 25% full-year growth while navigating the trough in EV adoption curves projected by BloombergNEF at 18% CAGR through 2027.

As we dive into the financials further, I'd like to spend some time on one of the most critical levers driving our profitability and market leadership in the EV space: battery costs per kilowatt-hour, or kWh. This metric is the lifeblood of our cost structure, directly impacting our vehicle gross margins, which came in at 24.2% this quarter—up 310 basis points year-over-year when adjusted for software mix.

In Q3, we achieved an average pack-level cost of $112 per kWh, a 6% sequential reduction from $119/kWh in Q2 and a robust 19% year-over-year decline from $138/kWh in Q3 2023. This puts us ahead of the North American industry average of $125/kWh, per our internal benchmarking against peers like Rivian and Lucid, and closing the gap with Tesla's reported sub-$110/kWh for their 4680-enabled packs.

To give you context, at the cell level, our costs are running at $68/kWh, down from $75/kWh a year ago, thanks to optimized sourcing from our key suppliers: CATL for LFP cells at around $55/kWh landed cost, LG Energy Solution for NMC at $72/kWh, and Panasonic for our high-nickel NCA cells in premium models. The pack premium—covering modules, BMS, cooling, and integration—has compressed to just 65% of cell cost, or about $44/kWh, driven by our adoption of cell-to-pack (CTP) architectures. For reference, legacy module-based packs carry a 90-100% premium, so this is a game-changer.

On trends: The industry has seen pack costs plummet from over $1,000/kWh in 2010 to today's levels, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of negative 18% over the past decade, per BloombergNEF data. We're projecting a continuation of 12-15% annual declines through 2027, targeting sub-$80/kWh pack costs by then. This aligns with BNEF's latest forecast of $75/kWh globally by 2025 and $58/kWh by 2030. Key inflection points include scale economies where global cell production hit 1.2 TWh in 2023, up 40% YoY, with utilization rates now at 75% versus 55% two years ago—our own Gigafactory Nevada Phase 2 ramped to 50 GWh annualized output this quarter, yielding a 22% cost reduction from learning curve effects alone; chemistry shifts with LFP adoption exploding from 15% of our packs in 2022 to 42% now, slashing costs by 25-30% versus NMC while enabling 400+ Wh/kg densities in CATL's latest Qilin cells—we've qualified Shenxing LFP for our mid-range Atlas SUV, dropping its pack cost to $62/kWh and extending range to 520 miles EPA; and manufacturing innovations like dry electrode coating, which we've piloted with our joint venture partner in South Carolina, cuts slurry costs by 40% and CapEx by 25%; silicon-dominant anodes, like those in our next-gen 46-series cells, promise 20% higher energy density at similar costs; and solid-state pilots—our R&D with QuantumScape targets 2027 production at $90/kWh with 800 Wh/L.

Regionally, the picture is bifurcated. In China, CATL and BYD dominate with cell costs at $52-58/kWh, fueled by overcapacity and state subsidies—BYD's Blade 2.0 LFP is sub-$50/kWh at scale. Europe lags at $135/kWh due to higher labor and raw material tariffs post-Ukraine, though Northvolt's Skellefteå ramp is helping. Here in the US, IRA localization credits have been transformative: our 75% domestic content in Nevada packs qualifies for the full $45/kWh PTC, effectively netting us $67/kWh post-incentive. Without IRA, US costs would mirror Europe's; with it, we're 20% below global averages.

Strategically, this cost trajectory is unlocking outsized margins. Every $10/kWh drop flows straight to 1.5-2% vehicle margin expansion, per our models. We're leveraging this through vertical integration: 60% of our 2024 packs will be in-house or JV-sourced, versus 30% in 2022, insulating us from supplier pricing volatility amid lithium carbonate swings (down 70% YTD to $12,000/tonne). Partnerships like our expanded CATL deal for 200 GWh LFP through 2028 lock in $60/kWh floors, while hedging 40% of cathode precursors mitigates nickel and cobalt risks.

Looking ahead, risks include supply chain chokepoints—refined graphite shortages could add $5-7/kWh if China export curbs tighten—and potential IRA clawbacks under policy shifts. But our upside is massive: at $80/kWh packs, our $35k Equinox EV competitor hits 30% margins, undercutting Tesla Model 3 by $3,000 on BOM. We're on track for $100/kWh enterprise-wide by EOY 2025, positioning Apex EV as the low-cost leader in a 20 million unit global EV market.

Finally, on our charging network expansion and utilization rates, we've added 1,200 new SuperCharge stalls globally, bringing our total to 8,500, with North America now at 65% utilization driven by Thunderbolt owners averaging 2.3 sessions per week. This supports seamless customer experience as adoption accelerates.

Now, I'll hand the call back to the operator for the Q&A session.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star then one. Our first question comes from John Smith with Morgan Stanley. Please go ahead.

Analyst 1:
Thanks, and good morning. Mike, great details on production. Can you elaborate on the Texas Gigafactory ramp and any bottlenecks for Q4 utilization targets?

Alex Rivera:
Thanks, John. The Texas site is performing exceptionally, hitting 97% utilization on Thunderbolt lines thanks to localized 4680 production and gigacasting. Minor semiconductor hiccups trimmed a few thousand units, but our dual-sourcing has us on track for 92-94% overall in Q4. We're confident in the 330k-340k volume guide.

Operator:
Our next question from Lisa Chen with Goldman Sachs.

Analyst 2:
Good morning. Mike, on pricing, with ASP down 9% sequentially, how do you see stabilization playing out amid China price wars, and what's the margin impact from promos?

Mike Chen:
Hi Lisa. ASP should stabilize at $52,500 in Q4 as Apex X ramps higher-margin mix. China deflation is a risk—BYD cuts could erode 20% industry-wide—but our vertical integration and AI dynamic pricing give us elasticity. Promos moderate to 4.5% of ASP, supporting 19.5-20.5% vehicle margins.

Operator:
Next from David Lee with JPMorgan.

Analyst 3:
Thanks. Alex, battery costs at $112/kWh are impressive. What's the outlook for LFP adoption and IRA dependency?

Alex Rivera:
David, LFP is now 42% of packs, enabling 520-mile range at $62/kWh for Atlas. IRA's $45/kWh PTC nets us $67/kWh effectively, but 60% in-house/JV sourcing de-risks policy shifts. Sub-$100/kWh by EOY '25 is locked in.

Sarah Johnson:
Thank you for your questions. We have time for one more.

Operator:
Our final question from Emily Park with Barclays.

Analyst 4:
Morning, team. On charging network, utilization is up—any plans to partner for fleet expansion, and how does this tie to FSD take rates?

Mike Chen:
Emily, 65% NA utilization reflects strong Thunderbolt usage. We're eyeing fleet partnerships like Hertz for dedicated stalls, which bundles with Autonomy Suite—FSD take rate at 28% added $1.1B high-margin revenue. Roadmap aligns charging with Level 3 autonomy rollout.

Operator:
Thank you. I would now like to turn the call back to Alex Rivera for closing remarks.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, operator, and thank you all for joining us today. We are confident that Apex EV Inc. is well-positioned for continued success in the rapidly evolving automotive landscape. We look forward to updating you on our progress next quarter.

Sarah Johnson:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes the Apex EV Inc. Q3 2024 earnings call. You may now disconnect.
